summary.text: An alloy is a mixture of chemical elements, at least one of them a metal, that retains the characteristics of a metal.
Alloying often gives properties different from the pure elements, such as increased strength, hardness or corrosion resistance.
In an alloy the atoms are joined by metallic bonding rather than the covalent bonds typically found in chemical compounds.

facts.label: Bronze
facts.value: Tin and copper, stronger and harder than either

facts.label: Steel
facts.value: Iron with a small amount of non-metallic carbon

facts.label: Stainless steel
facts.value: Steel with chromium added resists corrosion

facts.label: Natural alloy
facts.value: Electrum, silver and gold, occurs naturally

items.prompt: A toolmaker finds a pure metal too soft for the job. What might alloying do?

options.label: Make it lighter by mixing in a gas
Make it a covalent compound with new bonds
Make it stronger or harder by mixing in another element
Make it lose its metal characteristics entirely

items.explain: The vast majority of commercial metals are alloyed to improve properties such as strength, hardness or corrosion resistance.

items.prompt: Aluminium and copper are both very soft and ductile. What do you get if you alloy them together?

options.label: A much stronger material, even though both parents are soft
A material even softer than either parent
A material with exactly the average strength of the two
A material that is no longer a metal

items.explain: Although both metals are very soft and ductile, the resulting aluminium–copper alloy will have much greater strength.

items.prompt: A blacksmith adds a little carbon to iron. What trade is being made?

options.label: Iron's strength is given up for greater ductility
Iron gains both strength and ductility at no cost
Iron's hardness is given up for lower cost
Iron's great ductility is given up for greater strength

items.explain: Adding a small amount of non-metallic carbon to iron trades its great ductility for the greater strength of an alloy called steel.

items.prompt: You keep dissolving more of a second element into a molten metal. Eventually what happens?

options.label: It keeps dissolving without limit, making the alloy ever stronger
The constituent reaches a saturation point beyond which no more can be added
It turns into a gas and bubbles away
It forces the base metal to change into another element

items.explain: Even when constituents are soluble, each will usually have a saturation point, beyond which no more of the constituent can be added.

items.prompt: A molten mix cools and its constituents stay dissolved in each other. What kind of structure results?

options.label: Two or more types of crystals with different compositions
A layer of pure base metal with the extra on top
A liquid that never fully hardens
A solid solution of identical crystals, called a single phase

items.explain: If the metals remain soluble when solid, the alloy forms a solid solution, a homogeneous structure of identical crystals. If they become insoluble, they may separate into different crystal types.

items.prompt: Apart from improving properties, why might a maker mix copper into gold?

options.label: To lower the overall cost of the metal
To make the gold dissolve in acid
To turn the gold into a chemical compound
To stop gold bonding in a metallic way

items.explain: Metals may also be alloyed to reduce their overall cost, for instance alloys of gold and copper.
